Course 13

The mind in groups

Social psychology: how others influence us, why we obey, how prejudice arises and when we help.

Lesson 2. Obedience and roles

1 · Lesson

In the 1960s, Stanley Milgram asked volunteers to give what they believed were electric shocks to another person each time they made a mistake. Most went up to the maximum shock when urged by an experimenter in a lab coat, although many did so in visible distress. The shocks were not real.

Milgram's studies showed that obedience rises with the closeness and legitimacy of authority and falls when the victim is closer or when others refuse. They have been heavily debated, on ethical grounds and for how they were run, but their general message has been replicated in milder versions.

The Stanford prison experiment (Zimbardo, 1971) is often cited to claim that roles transform us. Today it is regarded as highly questionable: the "guards" were coached and the study does not meet scientific standards. It is a good reminder that famous studies must be read critically too.

2 · Example

In one of Milgram's variants, when two fake participants refused to continue, most volunteers stopped too. As with conformity, seeing someone disobey makes it easier to do so.

3 · Activity

Think of a rule at your work or in your circle that is followed without anyone questioning it. Do you know why it exists? Write what would happen if someone asked out loud.
